versions.text:
The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas looked over the blossoms on the corner tree first, the old tree his father had planted by the gate, and then read the thermometer nailed to the gate. After that he walked down to the young trees in the far row and came back by the barn to count the cans of oil: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard.

His plan was a ring of burners round the corner tree, which gave the best fruit on the place, and the rest in the far row, where he thought the cold settled first. He drew the loaded cart down from the barn himself, and I helped him set each burner with care.

Only then did he look across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard. She had judged that the cold would hold off until her trees were past blossom, and had let her oil order wait; now she stood at her gate with forty trees and nothing to light them with. Tomas pulled the burners out of the ring round the corner tree, put half the cans back on the cart, and called across that they would share what there was. I went with him to help.

We spent the night carrying oil across the lane wherever it was needed, guarding two orchards with one orchard's oil. The corner tree, out of reach of every burner now, stood pale and alone in the dark. Near four the frost was white on the lane and the thermometer touched minus five.

By morning Mrs. Odell's trees had come through, and the far row was saved. The corner tree had lost every blossom below the height of a man. The radio put the next frost in April, after the fruit had set, so the burners would wait in the barn until next spring before being lit again. Still in his boots, Tomas was back across the lane to ask how her trees had fared. If anyone asks me what kind of man my uncle is, I tell them about that morning.

The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas went out to the barn first to count the cans of oil: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard. Then he read the thermometer nailed to the gate, looked over the blossoms on the corner tree, the old tree his father had planted by the gate, and walked down to the young trees in the far row. Last, he looked across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard.

His plan was to keep every burner in a ring round the corner tree. It gave the best fruit on the place; his father had planted it, but it was the crop he thought of. I helped him set the burners out with care. The first flames drew moths out of the dark by the hundred.

Mrs. Odell came across the lane at eleven. She had judged the cold on that hillside for forty years, and she warned him that it would pool in the hollow, where his far row and her lowest trees stood side by side. She asked him to share the burners along the hollow and let the old tree take its chances, and offered to help. Tomas heard her out, thanked her, and kept to his plan. She went back and lit her own orchard with her own oil.

Near four the thermometer on the gate read minus three, but down in the hollow the frost was white on the grass. Inside the ring the corner tree stood bright, out of the cold's reach, and Tomas spent the night guarding it.

By morning the corner tree had come through and the far row was lost. Mrs. Odell's low trees, under her own burners, were saved. The radio put the next frost weeks away, past any need to light the burners again. Tomas said the forecast had been two degrees out, and sent me alone to count the dead trees while he raked under the corner tree. It had been Mrs. Odell, and not the radio, who had told him where the cold would go.

The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas went out first to read the thermometer nailed to the gate. From there he looked over the blossoms on the corner tree, the old tree his father had planted by the gate, walked down to the young trees in the far row, and went on to the barn to count the cans of oil: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard. Last of all he looked across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard.

After supper he drew a plan of the rows on the back of an envelope: a ring of burners round the corner tree, which gave the best fruit on the place, and a double line down the far row, where he thought the cold would settle. The plan needed fifteen cans. The other four, he said, would come across the lane.

They came at nine, in Mrs. Odell's wheelbarrow. Her own trees stood up on the ridge, above the cold, and she had judged that her oil would do more good shared. She had come to help, and she stayed. Between her cans and his, the burners reached every tree on the place, and after midnight it was she who kept them lit until dawn.

Near two, Mrs. Odell judged that the worst of the cold was over and wanted to let the far row burn down. Tomas kept it going, guarding the hollow with care, and at four, when the frost lay white and the thermometer touched minus five, the far row would have been lost without it.

By morning every tree had come through: the whole orchard saved. The cans were empty. Then the radio put the next frost on Friday, and the oil truck could not come until Monday. I was to take the train home on Thursday, and Mrs. Odell would be at her sister's. Tomas had coughed through most of the night, and he was still coughing as he stacked the empty cans by the barn door. On Thursday, from the train, I could see the cans by the barn and, below them, the far row white with blossom in the hollow where the cold would settle.

The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas went to the window first and looked across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard. Then he read the thermometer nailed to the gate and walked down to the young trees in the far row. In the barn he counted the cans of oil: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard. He came back last to look over the blossoms on the corner tree his father had planted by the gate.

The old tree had given little fruit for years, and the best of it went to the birds. It would not come through this one, Tomas thought, whatever we did. Still, his plan put two-thirds of the burners in a ring round it, each set with care, and the rest reached only down the far row, where the cold settled first. Tomas and I drew straws for the first watch.

Mrs. Odell came across the lane at eleven. Her own orchard was lit with her own oil. She had come to share the watch and help, but Tomas sat her beside him instead. She remembered his father planting the corner tree the spring the lane was graveled, carrying it up from the station in a bucket.

Toward dawn the frost came down harder than the radio had warned, and the thermometer on the gate read minus five. Both of them had judged that the old tree would be lost, and neither left it. Tomas spent the last hours guarding it, refilling each burner as it needed oil.

By morning the far row had come through, saved by the few burners we could spare it. The blossoms on the corner tree were brown by noon. The next frost held off until the fruit had set, and the burners stayed in the barn until they were lit again the next spring. Tomas cut the old tree down that winter. I still keep a twig of it pressed in a book, taken at midnight, when it stood white in the ring of flame and Mrs. Odell was telling us about the bucket.

The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas walked down first to the young trees in the far row. On the way back he counted the cans of oil in the barn: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard. Then he read the thermometer nailed to the gate, looked over the blossoms on the corner tree, the old tree his father had planted by the gate, and looked across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard.

His plan put a ring of burners round the far row and a double line through the middle of the orchard, as far as eleven cans would reach, which was all it needed. The corner tree gave the best fruit on the place, but it stood too far off and was left to itself. When I had helped him light every burner, each set with care, Tomas drew a long breath at the gate and said the frost would have to get past him first.

Mrs. Odell came across the lane at ten with a notebook. Her own orchard was lit with her own oil; she had come to share the watch. Both of them judged the cold would go to minus six. All night she read the thermometer every quarter hour and wrote it down, while Tomas, whose burners were all lit and trimmed, nodded at each figure.

The readings went minus one, minus one, zero, minus one. By three Tomas had walked the ring forty times, guarding the far row with an oil can in each hand. Out by the gate the corner tree stood in the dark, beyond the reach of any flame.

By morning every tree had come through, and the corner tree, forty yards from the nearest burner, had the best blossom on the place. The radio put the next frost in April, after the fruit had set, so the burners would be lit again only the next spring. Tomas thought the burners had saved the orchard from being lost, and in June he said so again as he passed round the first bowl of apricots. Every one of them came from the corner tree.
